hints: Focus on how the top and bottom numbers tell you different things, protons plus neutrons versus just protons.
Work out ion 1 first, neutrons are 19 minus 9 = 10, and electrons are 9 plus 1 for the 1- charge = 10.
Now apply the same two rules to the others, neutrons = mass minus proton number and electrons = protons minus charge, and see which ones match.
walkthrough:
**Recall the two counting rules**

Great start, let us get the tools clear. Neutrons do not care about charge, electrons do.

$$\text{neutrons} = \text{mass number} - \text{proton number}$$ $$\text{electrons in ion} = \text{proton number} - \text{ion charge}$$

**Check ion 1, $^{19}_{9}\text{F}^{-}$**

Fluorine has 9 protons. Neutrons = 19 - 9 = 10. The 1- charge means one extra electron, so electrons = 9 + 1 = 10.

$$10 \text{ neutrons} = 10 \text{ electrons, so 1 is correct}$$

**Check ion 2, $^{31}_{15}\text{P}^{-}$**

Phosphorus has 15 protons. Neutrons = 31 - 15 = 16. Again a 1- charge adds one electron, so electrons = 15 + 1 = 16.

$$16 \text{ neutrons} = 16 \text{ electrons, so 2 is correct}$$

**Check ion 3, $^{23}_{11}\text{Na}^{+}$**

Sodium has 11 protons. Neutrons = 23 - 11 = 12. But a 1+ charge means one electron lost, so electrons = 11 - 1 = 10.

$$12 \text{ neutrons} \neq 10 \text{ electrons, so 3 is incorrect}$$

**Combine the conclusion**

Only 1 and 2 have equal electrons and neutrons. That matches the 1 and 2 only combination.

options.A: This says 1, 2 and 3 are all correct. But 3 is wrong because $^{23}_{11}\text{Na}^{+}$ has 12 neutrons and only 10 electrons. Students choose this if they forget a positive ion loses electrons and count 11 electrons instead of 10.
options.B: This says 1 and 2 only, which is perfect. Both $^{19}_{9}\text{F}^{-}$ (10 and 10) and $^{31}_{15}\text{P}^{-}$ (16 and 16) have electrons equal to neutrons, while 3 does not.
options.C: This says 2 and 3 only. Ion 2 is correct, but ion 3 is incorrect (12 neutrons vs 10 electrons) and ion 1 is missed even though it clearly matches (10 vs 10).
options.D: This says 1 only. Ion 1 is correct, but ion 2 is also correct and is missed. Students choose this if they make an arithmetic slip like 31 minus 15 = 15 or forget to add the extra electron for $\text{P}^{-}$.
